projectTitle: Wrenfield Logistics: The Document That Talked Back
projectTagline: A 20-video, start-to-finish RAG build for a fictional logistics company -- a real internal knowledge assistant taken from document ingestion through Azure AI Search, GPT-4o, and a Docker deployment, then put through a genuine red-team security review that catches an indirect prompt-injection vulnerability before it reaches real employees.
businessContext: Wrenfield Logistics is a mid-size logistics and supply-chain company with about 2,200 employees. HR, IT Support, and Operations each field the same repeat questions by email and Slack -- benefits, VPN resets, shipping exceptions -- even though the real answers already exist in written policies, wiki pages, and SOPs nobody can find fast enough. Priya Desai (HR) and Omar Haddad (IT Support) want an assistant that actually answers from those real documents; Jordan Vance (AI Engineer) builds it, Caleb Shaw (DevOps) deploys it, and Lena Ortiz (Security & Compliance) runs the security review that finds a real indirect prompt-injection vulnerability hiding in a stale, forgotten document before it does any real damage.
architectureSummary: Azure Blob Storage (`wrenfield-knowledge-docs`) holding three real document sets -- HR policies, IT wiki pages, and Ops SOPs; a Python ingestion/chunking pipeline (~500-token chunks, 50-token overlap); Azure OpenAI `text-embedding-3-small` embeddings indexed into Azure AI Search (`wrenfield-knowledge-index`, hybrid vector+keyword search, top-k=5); Azure OpenAI GPT-4o generation grounded in retrieved context, with citations and a real 'I don't know' fallback; a Python FastAPI service (`/ask`) containerized with Docker and deployed to Azure Container Apps. A standing red-team eval suite and hardened system prompt now guard against indirect prompt injection from retrieved document content.

lessons.title: Meeting Wrenfield: The Same Questions, Every Day
lessons.summary: The discovery meeting: HR, IT Support, and Operations each field the same repeat questions every single day, even though the real answers already exist in Wrenfield's own written documents -- and where those documents actually live.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Over the next 20 videos, you'll walk through one complete, start-to-finish AI engineering build for a fictional logistics/supply-chain company, **Wrenfield Logistics** -- about 2,200 employees, moving freight and managing warehouses across multiple sites. Wrenfield doesn't have a knowledge problem in the sense of missing information. It has a *findability* problem: the real answers to 'what's our parental leave policy,' 'how do I reset my VPN,' and 'what's the exception process for a damaged shipment' already exist, written down, somewhere in the company's own documents. They just aren't fast to find, so the same questions get asked over and over by email and Slack, to real people, every single day.
This video starts exactly where this kind of project always has to start: not with a model, not with a line of Python, but with a meeting where you find out precisely who feels this pain, how often, and where the real source documents actually live. You, **Jordan Vance**, are Wrenfield's AI Engineer -- the one building this project from here through the rest of the series. **Priya Desai**, Head of People Operations, is HR's business sponsor; she's tired of her small team re-answering the same benefits and leave questions that are already sitting in a PDF nobody can find fast enough. **Omar Haddad**, IT Support Lead, is the co-sponsor on the IT side -- his team's ticket queue is full of password resets and VPN setup questions that are already answered, word for word, on an internal wiki page. Operations has the same pattern, even though nobody from that team is in this first meeting yet: warehouse staff ask about shipping-exception procedures that already exist as written SOPs.
By the end of this series, Wrenfield has a working system that answers these questions from its own real documents, with citations, deployed to production. This lesson is step one: understanding exactly whose problem this is and exactly where the real data lives, before touching either a model or a line of code.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine a school with a giant filing cabinet that has the answer to almost every question a student could ask -- when the cafeteria opens, how to get a locker fixed, what to do if you lose your bus pass. The answers are all in there, typed up and correct. The problem is the filing cabinet is enormous, it isn't organized by question, and the only people who know roughly where to look are three very busy school staff members who get asked the same ten questions, out loud, all day long, instead of ever getting to just point at the right drawer.
That's Wrenfield Logistics right now. Priya Desai's HR team already wrote down the parental leave policy. Omar Haddad's IT team already wrote down how to reset a VPN. Somewhere in Operations, someone already wrote down what to do with a damaged shipment. None of that information is missing -- it's just buried in a filing cabinet too big and too disorganized for a busy employee to search through themselves, so they ask a person instead, every single day, forever. Your job starts with finding out exactly how big that filing cabinet really is, and exactly who keeps getting interrupted because of it.
lessons.explainProfessional:
The detail that matters most in this discovery meeting isn't 'people ask repeat questions' -- every support org on earth has that problem. It's that the ground truth already exists in written, structured document form, across three separate owners, and the failure mode is retrieval, not knowledge creation. That distinction is the whole reason this is a retrieval-augmented-generation problem and not a model-training problem: Wrenfield doesn't need a system that learns new facts, it needs a system that can find and surface facts that are already correct and already written down, fast enough to beat interrupting a person.
That's why this meeting has to end with a precise inventory, not just a complaint. Priya's team owns roughly 140 HR policy PDFs covering benefits, leave, and expense policy, stored in Azure Blob Storage under the `wrenfield-knowledge-docs` container, in the `hr-policies/` folder. Omar's team owns roughly 310 IT support wiki pages -- VPN setup, password reset, hardware requests -- exported from Confluence as HTML/markdown, sitting in that same container's `it-wiki/` folder. Operations owns roughly 95 SOP documents -- warehouse procedures, shipping exceptions -- in `ops-sops/`. All three live in the same blob container today, but under three different owners with three different update habits, which matters enormously later: whatever this project builds has to handle documents that change on different schedules, owned by people who were never in this first meeting together. Two more names matter for later lessons, even though their work hasn't started yet: **Lena Ortiz**, Security & Compliance Lead, will own the security review of whatever gets built here, and **Caleb Shaw**, Platform/DevOps Engineer, will support getting it deployed on Azure. Neither is in scope for this lesson -- this lesson is discovery, full stop.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Walk in already knowing what you don't know

Before meeting anyone, write down what you need to confirm, not just what you assume:

- Is this really the *same* small set of questions repeating, or does it just feel that way to the people answering them?
- Do the real answers already exist in writing somewhere, or are some of these 'tribal knowledge' that nobody has actually documented?
- Where do the documents that do exist actually live, physically, and who owns keeping each set current?

## Step 2 -- Meet Priya Desai and get HR's version of the problem

```
PRIYA:   My team answers the same twenty questions every week by email.
         'What's our parental leave policy,' 'how many PTO days do I
         have left,' 'what's covered under the expense policy.' Every
         one of those answers is already written down. We have about
         140 policy PDFs. Nobody on my team wants to be the human
         search engine for documents we already wrote.

JORDAN:  When an employee asks you one of these, where do you actually
         go to find the answer yourself?

PRIYA:   Honestly, I search a shared folder by filename and hope I
         remember which PDF has it. New hires on my team take weeks
         to learn where things are.
```

## Step 3 -- Meet Omar Haddad and get IT's version of the problem

```
OMAR:    Same story, different documents. My ticket queue is full of
         'how do I reset my VPN,' 'how do I request new hardware,'
         'my password won't reset.' All of it is already written up
         on our internal wiki -- about 310 pages, exported out of
         Confluence as HTML and markdown. My team spends real hours a
         week just re-typing links to pages that already answer the
         question.

JORDAN:  And Operations has the same pattern?

OMAR:    From what I hear, yes -- damaged-shipment exceptions, warehouse
         procedure questions. Nobody from Ops is in this meeting yet,
         but I'd bet their ticket pattern looks identical to mine.
```

## Step 4 -- Confirm where the documents actually live

Ask Priya and Omar directly, and get this exact inventory in writing:

```
Storage:   Azure Blob Storage, container `wrenfield-knowledge-docs`

hr-policies/   ~140 HR policy PDFs (benefits, leave, expense policy)
               owned by Priya Desai's team
it-wiki/       ~310 IT support wiki pages, exported from Confluence
               as HTML/markdown (VPN setup, password reset,
               hardware requests) -- owned by Omar Haddad's team
ops-sops/      ~95 Operations SOP documents (warehouse procedures,
               shipping exceptions) -- owned by Operations
```

## Step 5 -- Write the discovery summary while it's fresh

```
WRENFIELD LOGISTICS -- DISCOVERY SUMMARY

Business problem:   HR, IT Support, and Operations each field the
                     same repeat questions by email/Slack every day,
                     even though the real answers already exist in
                     written documents.
Sponsors:            Priya Desai (HR), Omar Haddad (IT Support).
Source of truth:     Azure Blob Storage, container
                     wrenfield-knowledge-docs -- hr-policies/ (~140
                     PDFs), it-wiki/ (~310 pages), ops-sops/ (~95
                     docs). Three different owners, three different
                     update cadences.
Later involvement:   Lena Ortiz (Security & Compliance) will review
                     this once something is built; Caleb Shaw
                     (Platform/DevOps) will support the Azure
                     deployment. Neither is active yet.
```

## Step 6 -- Confirm it in writing with Priya and Omar

Send this summary to both and ask directly: 'Did I capture this accurately, and did I get your document counts and folder names right?' Every requirement you write in the next lesson traces back to a line in this document -- and getting the real folder names right now, `hr-policies/`, `it-wiki/`, `ops-sops/`, is what keeps every later lesson's pipeline pointed at the real thing instead of a guess.

No warehouse or search index exists yet -- these are just files sitting in blob storage today, owned by three teams with three different update cadences.

lessons.title: Turning 'Answer From Our Docs' Into a Testable Requirement
lessons.summary: Converting 'just answer questions from our documents' into one precise, testable requirement: answers must be grounded in and cite the real source documents, must say 'I don't know' when the docs don't cover something, and must be fast enough to actually beat asking a person.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Discovery gave you a real problem and a real inventory of documents -- but 'just answer questions from our docs' isn't a requirement yet, it's an intention. It doesn't say what happens when the docs don't have an answer, it doesn't say how a reader is supposed to trust the answer is actually correct, and it doesn't say how fast is fast enough to matter. This lesson turns that intention into three testable conditions that this entire series builds toward.
The requirement this lesson locks in has three parts, and all three were argued out loud with Priya Desai and Omar Haddad, not assumed: every answer must be grounded in the real documents in `hr-policies/`, `it-wiki/`, and `ops-sops/` and must cite which document it came from -- never invented; when the documents genuinely don't cover a question, the system must say so instead of guessing; and an answer has to arrive fast enough that asking the system is actually faster than interrupting a person on Priya's or Omar's team. Every later lesson -- the chunking pipeline, the index, the generation step, the API -- answers to this exact definition.
lessons.explainSimple:
Remember the giant filing cabinet? Once everyone agrees they want a faster way to search it, somebody still has to answer a harder question: what happens if someone asks about a drawer that was never filled? A good helper at the filing cabinet doesn't make up an answer just to seem useful -- it says 'I don't have that on file' and stops there. And the helper only matters if it's actually faster than walking down the hall and asking a real person.
That's what this lesson nails down for Wrenfield. Instead of 'answer questions from our docs,' the real rule becomes: every answer has to point at the exact document it came from, so nobody has to just trust it blindly; if the filing cabinet genuinely doesn't have the answer, the helper has to say so instead of inventing one; and the whole thing only counts as useful if it answers faster than emailing Priya's or Omar's team and waiting for a reply.
lessons.explainProfessional:
A requirement that can't be falsified isn't a requirement, it's a hope -- and 'answer questions from our docs' is exactly that until it's pinned to a precise grounding behavior, an explicit abstention behavior, and a measurable latency bar. All three matter independently, and all three were missing from the original ask.
Groundedness has to be defined as a behavior, not a vibe: every answer the system produces must be traceable to specific passages in the real source documents under `hr-policies/`, `it-wiki/`, or `ops-sops/`, and the response has to cite which document (and ideally which section) it drew from. This is the property that later lessons call retrieval-augmented generation -- the model is never allowed to answer purely from what it 'remembers' from pretraining, because an invented-sounding-plausible HR policy answer is worse than no answer at all; it's actively dangerous in an HR or compliance context. The second condition, abstention, is the harder one to get stakeholders to actually commit to in writing: when none of the retrieved passages cover the question, the system must say it doesn't know rather than let the generation model smooth over the gap with a plausible-sounding guess. This has to be an explicit, agreed requirement now, because it's the one a team under deadline pressure is most tempted to quietly relax later. The third condition, latency, is what makes this project worth building at all rather than just a nicer search box -- the system has to beat the real alternative, which is interrupting a specific person on Priya's or Omar's team and waiting for a reply, not some abstract target. Note what this lesson deliberately does not yet claim: nothing here states a specific accuracy number or adoption number. Those are honest open questions this project is setting up the requirements to be tested against later, not answering yet.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Pull the real constraint out of both sponsors

```
JORDAN:  You both want this to 'answer questions from our docs.' What
         happens today when someone on your team gets asked something
         that genuinely isn't written down anywhere?

PRIYA:   Honestly, sometimes we guess, based on how we think policy
         should work, and it's not always right. That's actually
         worse than just saying 'I'll check and get back to you.'

OMAR:    Same on the IT side. I'd much rather a tool say 'I don't
         know' than confidently make something up about a VPN
         setting that turns out to be wrong.
```

## Step 2 -- Fix the exact requirement in writing

This is the definition every later lesson in this series refers back to:

```
WRENFIELD KNOWLEDGE ASSISTANT -- V1 REQUIREMENT

REQ-1 (Groundedness): Every answer must be derived from, and must
       cite, specific passages in the real source documents under
       hr-policies/, it-wiki/, or ops-sops/ in the
       wrenfield-knowledge-docs container. The system must never
       answer from general knowledge alone.

REQ-2 (Abstention): When the retrieved documents do not contain an
       answer to the question, the system must say it does not
       know, rather than generate a plausible-sounding guess.

REQ-3 (Speed): An answer must arrive fast enough that using the
       system is actually faster than emailing or Slack-messaging a
       person on Priya's or Omar's team and waiting for a reply.
```

## Step 3 -- Stress-test the requirement with real examples

Before trusting this requirement, run through it with concrete sample questions from each document set:

```
- 'What's our parental leave policy?' -- should be answered from
  hr-policies/, with a citation to the specific PDF.
- 'How do I reset my VPN?' -- should be answered from it-wiki/, with
  a citation to the specific wiki page.
- 'What's the exception process for a damaged shipment?' -- should
  be answered from ops-sops/, with a citation to the specific SOP.
- 'What's our policy on remote work in Portugal?' (a made-up edge
  case, if nothing in hr-policies/ actually covers it) -- should
  trigger REQ-2 and say so, not guess.
```

Walk a handful of real questions past Priya and Omar and ask them directly whether the citation each answer would need to point to actually exists in their folders -- that's what keeps REQ-1 honest.

## Step 4 -- Agree on what 'fast enough' means in practice

```
OMAR:    How fast are we talking? My team can usually answer a quick
         ticket in a few minutes if they're not swamped, longer if
         they are.

JORDAN:  The target is answers landing in a few seconds, not minutes
         -- comfortably faster than opening a ticket or waiting on a
         Slack reply, even on a good day.

PRIYA:   If it's genuinely faster than asking a person, my team will
         actually point employees at it instead of just answering
         directly out of habit.
```

## Step 5 -- Write the requirement and get it signed off

Save the REQ-1/REQ-2/REQ-3 block above as `Wrenfield_V1_Requirement_v1.md`, alongside the Lesson 1 discovery summary. Get explicit sign-off from Priya and Omar on all three conditions, especially REQ-2 -- abstention is the one most likely to get quietly dropped later once a demo looks impressive, and it's the one this whole series is built to protect.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Locked the exact requirement: every answer must be grounded in and cite the real source documents under hr-policies/, it-wiki/, or ops-sops/ (REQ-1); the system must explicitly say it doesn't know when the docs don't cover a question, never guess (REQ-2); and answers must land fast enough to beat asking a person, on the order of seconds (REQ-3). No accuracy or adoption numbers are being claimed yet -- those get tested honestly once there's a real system to measure.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: We converted 'answer questions from our docs' into three precise, written requirements -- grounded and cited answers, honest 'I don't know' when the docs don't cover something, and speed that actually beats asking a person -- all signed off by Priya and Omar. This is the document every later pipeline, index, and API decision in this project gets measured against.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We've turned a vague goal into a specific, testable commitment: answers that are always traceable back to our real policies and procedures, that admit when they don't know something instead of guessing, and that are fast enough to actually change how people get help. We aren't yet claiming how well it performs -- that gets proven honestly as the project moves forward.

lessons.title: Scoping V1: Three Real Document Sets, Not a Company-Wide AI
lessons.summary: Drawing a hard written line around what V1 actually ships -- answers grounded in hr-policies/, it-wiki/, and ops-sops/ only -- and naming what's explicitly deferred: connecting to every system at Wrenfield, taking actions on a user's behalf, and replacing judgment calls that HR, IT, or Ops staff have to make.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
You now have a precise, signed-off requirement. Before any pipeline gets built or any model gets called, this lesson draws a hard written line around what V1 of this project actually delivers -- and, just as importantly, what it explicitly does not. For Wrenfield, V1 ships exactly one thing: a question-answering system grounded in the three real document sets named in Lesson 1 -- `hr-policies/` (~140 PDFs), `it-wiki/` (~310 wiki pages), and `ops-sops/` (~95 SOPs) -- that meets the REQ-1/REQ-2/REQ-3 requirement from Lesson 2.
What's explicitly out of scope for V1, named in writing rather than left to assumption, is anything beyond answering from those three document sets. V1 does not connect to every system at Wrenfield -- not payroll, not the shipment-tracking system, not the HRIS itself, just the documents in `wrenfield-knowledge-docs`. V1 does not take any action on a user's behalf -- it does not reset a VPN, does not file an expense report, does not open or close a support ticket. And V1 does not replace HR, IT, or Operations staff for anything that requires human judgment -- a genuinely ambiguous leave-policy edge case, a security exception, a judgment call on a damaged shipment still goes to a person. Naming these now as deferred, not ignored, is what keeps this project from quietly growing into a company-wide AI platform before it's shipped one working answer.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine a reference librarian who is extremely good at exactly one job: finding the right page in the right book and reading it back to you, with the page number, so you can trust it. A reference librarian who also tried to check out your books for you, drive you home, and decide whether your overdue-book excuse was good enough would be a worse librarian -- slower, more likely to make a mistake, and harder to trust for the one job that actually matters.
This project is Wrenfield's reference librarian for three specific bookshelves: HR policies, the IT wiki, and the Operations SOPs. It finds the right page and reads it back with a citation. It does not reset anyone's VPN, it does not file paperwork, and it definitely does not decide a genuinely hard judgment call instead of a real person. Those are real jobs for real people to keep doing -- the librarian's job is just to make the easy, already-answered questions fast.
lessons.explainProfessional:
Scope discipline matters here specifically because a working document Q&A system is an unusually tempting thing to over-promise on once it exists. The moment it can answer 'how do I reset my VPN' correctly, it's natural for a stakeholder to ask 'can it also just reset it for me?' or 'can it also pull from the HRIS directly, so it knows my actual PTO balance?' Both are reasonable asks and both are real future work -- and both would, if bundled into V1, turn a well-scoped retrieval-and-answer system into an open-ended agentic-actions and systems-integration project with no clear finish line.
The deferral has to be specific and honest, not a vague 'later.' Taking actions on a user's behalf -- resetting a VPN, filing an expense report, opening a ticket -- is deferred because granting an AI system write access to real systems is a fundamentally different risk profile than read-only question answering, and nobody has designed, or security-reviewed, that risk yet; Lena Ortiz's security review (still ahead in this series) is squarely about the system that exists, not a hypothetical action-taking one. Replacing human judgment on ambiguous cases is deferred because the REQ-2 abstention requirement from Lesson 2 already defines the boundary: when a question is genuinely ambiguous or outside what the three document sets cover, the right behavior is saying so, not guessing on behalf of a person who would otherwise make that call. Connecting to every other system at Wrenfield is deferred because it multiplies the integration surface and the security review scope for every system added, with no requirement from Lesson 2 that currently demands it. What V1 commits to is narrower and fully ownable: grounded, cited answers from three specific, named document sets, nothing more.

lessons.title: Choosing the Stack: Azure OpenAI, Azure AI Search, and FastAPI
lessons.summary: The first real architecture decision: Azure Blob Storage for the source documents, a Python chunking pipeline, Azure OpenAI text-embedding-3-small for embeddings, Azure AI Search (hybrid vector + keyword, index wrenfield-knowledge-index, top-k=5) as the retrieval layer, Azure OpenAI GPT-4o for generation, and a FastAPI backend behind /ask, packaged in Docker and deployed to Azure Container Apps -- justified against real alternatives for Wrenfield's real constraints.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
With scope locked, this is the first real architecture decision: exactly what tools turn `hr-policies/`, `it-wiki/`, and `ops-sops/` into the grounded, cited, fast answers Lesson 2 and Lesson 3 committed to. The stack this series uses, and justifies in this lesson, is: **Azure Blob Storage** (container `wrenfield-knowledge-docs`) as the document source; a **Python chunking pipeline** that splits each document into roughly 500-token chunks with 50-token overlap; **Azure OpenAI**'s `text-embedding-3-small` model to turn each chunk into an embedding; **Azure AI Search** as the retrieval layer -- hybrid vector-plus-keyword search, index name `wrenfield-knowledge-index`, top-k=5 -- to find the most relevant chunks for a question; **Azure OpenAI GPT-4o** to generate the final answer from those retrieved chunks; a **Python FastAPI** backend exposing a single `/ask` endpoint that ties the retrieval and generation steps together; and **Docker** packaging deployed to **Azure Container Apps** for production, with **Caleb Shaw** supporting that deployment.
Each piece earns its place against a real alternative, not just convention. Azure AI Search's hybrid mode beats a pure-vector-only store because exact keyword matches genuinely matter at Wrenfield -- a policy name like 'Parental Leave Policy' or a specific extension number in the IT wiki needs to match on the literal text, not just semantic similarity, and a vector-only index can miss that. GPT-4o beats a smaller, cheaper model for the generation step because REQ-1 and REQ-2 from Lesson 2 depend on the model following grounding and abstention instructions reliably -- at this project's scale, instruction-following and groundedness quality matter more than shaving generation cost.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine you're setting up a lost-and-found desk at a school. You'd want a filing system that lets you search two ways: by the exact label on the item (like 'blue jacket, size medium') and by a fuzzy description (like 'warm coat, sort of blue-ish') in case someone doesn't remember the exact label. A system that only does fuzzy matching might miss the jacket someone described by its exact tag, and a system that only does exact matching might miss it if someone describes it loosely. You want both at once.
That's exactly why Wrenfield's search tool does both: it can match an exact policy name or an exact extension number, and it can also match a loosely worded question to the right document even if the wording isn't identical. And for writing the final answer, Wrenfield picked a smarter, more careful assistant over a faster-but-sloppier one, because getting the answer right and admitting when it doesn't know matters more here than saving a few cents per question.
lessons.explainProfessional:
Every choice in this stack traces back to a real constraint from the first three lessons, not a default. Start with retrieval: REQ-1 from Lesson 2 requires groundedness, which means retrieval quality is the ceiling on everything downstream -- generation can't cite a passage retrieval never surfaced. Wrenfield's documents contain a meaningful amount of exact-match-sensitive content: specific policy names, specific extension numbers, specific SOP codes in `ops-sops/`. A pure embedding-based vector store can under-rank a chunk that contains the exact string a user typed if that string isn't semantically distinctive on its own. **Azure AI Search**'s hybrid mode -- combining vector similarity over `text-embedding-3-small` embeddings with traditional keyword (BM25-style) scoring, over the index `wrenfield-knowledge-index` -- covers both failure modes at once, which a vector-only store like a bare vector database would not without bolting on a separate keyword layer itself. Top-k=5 is chosen as a starting point generous enough to usually include the right chunk for the generation step to cite, without flooding the prompt with irrelevant context that increases the odds of the model confusing sources.
Chunking at roughly 500 tokens with 50-token overlap is a deliberate middle ground: large enough that a chunk usually contains a complete policy clause or a complete wiki instruction rather than a fragment, small enough that retrieval stays precise and the generation prompt stays focused, with the 50-token overlap reducing the odds that a clause gets split exactly at a chunk boundary and becomes unretrievable from either side. Generation model choice follows directly from REQ-1 and REQ-2: this project needs a model that reliably follows a 'only answer from the provided context, and say you don't know if the context doesn't cover it' instruction, across HR, IT, and Ops content with very different tones and structures. **GPT-4o** is chosen over a smaller or cheaper model specifically because instruction-following and groundedness reliability matter more here than raw per-call cost -- a cheaper model that occasionally ignores the abstention instruction would directly violate REQ-2. Finally, a **Python FastAPI** backend behind a single `/ask` endpoint, packaged in **Docker** and deployed to **Azure Container Apps**, is chosen because it's a thin, well-understood layer that just orchestrates the retrieval and generation calls -- there's no requirement yet for anything heavier, and Container Apps gives Caleb Shaw a straightforward, container-based deployment target without managing raw virtual machines. None of this stack choice says anything yet about how well the resulting answers actually perform against REQ-1/REQ-2/REQ-3 -- that's a question this series answers honestly once there's a real pipeline and real evaluation to look at, not one to assume here.

lessons.title: Designing the Ingestion and Chunking Pipeline
lessons.summary: Deciding how Wrenfield's HR policies, IT wiki pages, and Ops SOPs actually get pulled out of Azure Blob Storage and cut into pieces small enough to embed and retrieve -- and why ingesting everything in each folder, with no manual curation, is the right V1 call rather than a shortcut.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
With the business problem and the stack settled, this lesson is where Jordan Vance designs the first real pipeline stage: getting Wrenfield's existing documents out of Azure Blob Storage and into pieces small enough for an embedding model to actually work with. The source is one container, `wrenfield-knowledge-docs`, split into three folders that map directly to the three teams drowning in repeat questions: `hr-policies/` (roughly 140 PDFs, owned by Priya Desai's team), `it-wiki/` (roughly 310 Confluence-exported wiki pages, owned by Omar Haddad's team), and `ops-sops/` (roughly 95 SOP documents).

The design decision this lesson commits to, in writing, is to ingest every file inside all three folders -- no manual review of which of the 545 documents are worth including, no curation pass, no filtering on anything beyond "is this a document in one of the three folders." That's deliberate: hand-reviewing 545 real documents before a single question has ever been answered would burn weeks nobody has budgeted, and nothing about the current folders suggests any of them need special handling yet. The other half of this lesson is the chunking approach itself -- roughly 500-token chunks with 50-token overlap -- and the metadata every chunk carries forward (filename, which folder it came from, and its position within the source document), because that metadata is what makes a cited answer possible two lessons from now.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine you've been handed three filing cabinets full of paper -- one of HR handbooks, one of IT troubleshooting notes, one of operations procedures -- and your job is to build a machine that can flip straight to the right paragraph when someone asks a question. You can't hand a computer an entire 40-page handbook and ask it to find one sentence; it works much better if you first cut every document into smaller index cards, each one a few hundred words, with a little bit of the previous card's ending repeated at the start of the next card so an idea that spans two cards doesn't get sliced in half.

That's the plan this lesson lays out: take every single page in all three filing cabinets, no exceptions, and turn it into index cards of about 500 words with a 50-word overlap between neighbors. Each index card also gets a sticky note on the back saying exactly which document it came from and roughly where in that document it sat -- because later, when the system answers someone's question, it needs to be able to say "here's where I got that" rather than just asserting an answer out of nowhere.
lessons.explainProfessional:
Two design decisions get fixed in this lesson, and both are chosen for concrete reasons rather than defaults. The first is scope: ingestion pulls every object under all three folder prefixes (`hr-policies/`, `it-wiki/`, `ops-sops/`) in `wrenfield-knowledge-docs`, with no filtering beyond folder membership. For a V1 knowledge pipeline, this is the right tradeoff -- building a review workflow to vet 545 documents before any retrieval has even been tested would delay the whole project for a benefit nobody has asked for, and Priya's, Omar's, and the Ops team's folders are their teams' normal working document stores, not an inbox of unreviewed submissions. The decision is written down explicitly as "ingest everything in the folder," rather than left as an implicit assumption, so it's a choice the team can revisit later if a real reason to filter ever turns up.

The second is chunk shape. Chunking at roughly 500 tokens with a 50-token overlap is a well-established middle ground for retrieval-augmented generation: large enough that a chunk usually contains a complete thought (a full policy clause, a full troubleshooting step) rather than a fragment, small enough that Azure AI Search's top-k=5 retrieval returns content that's actually dense with relevant material rather than mostly padding, and the 50-token overlap exists specifically so that an idea sitting across a chunk boundary -- the end of one policy paragraph and the start of the next -- isn't permanently split so that neither chunk contains the whole thing. Every chunk the pipeline produces carries three metadata fields forward: `filename` (the exact blob path), `source_set` (which of the three folders it came from -- `hr-policies`, `it-wiki`, or `ops-sops`), and a position marker (`page_number` for a PDF, `section` for a wiki export) -- because a retrieved chunk with no record of its origin can't be cited back to a real document, which the next lessons in this series depend on for both evaluation and user trust.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Confirm exactly what's in the container

Jordan starts by walking the real source with Priya and Omar rather than assuming its shape:

```text
Container: wrenfield-knowledge-docs

  hr-policies/   ~140 PDFs       (owned by Priya Desai's team)
  it-wiki/       ~310 pages      (Confluence export, owned by Omar Haddad's team)
  ops-sops/      ~95 documents   (Operations SOPs, PDF and Word)
```

Nobody on either team flags any document in their folder as unreliable, outdated, or not meant for general use -- these are the same folders HR, IT, and Ops already point employees to today, just not in a form anyone can search by asking a question.

## Step 2 -- Decide the ingestion scope in writing

```text
INGESTION SCOPE -- V1

Rule: ingest every file found under hr-policies/, it-wiki/, and
      ops-sops/ in wrenfield-knowledge-docs. No manual review of
      individual documents, no filtering beyond folder membership.

Why: these are each team's live working document stores, not an
      unreviewed inbox. Hand-vetting 545 documents before a single
      real question has been answered isn't a cost this project can
      justify yet, and nothing about the current folders suggests a
      need to.

Revisit if: a team flags a specific document as something that
      shouldn't be searchable, or ingestion surfaces something that
      changes this calculus.
```

## Step 3 -- Fix the chunking parameters

```text
CHUNK_SIZE   = 500 tokens
CHUNK_OVERLAP = 50 tokens
```

500 tokens is large enough to usually hold one complete policy clause or troubleshooting step, small enough that `wrenfield-knowledge-index`'s top-k=5 retrieval returns dense, relevant chunks instead of mostly filler. The 50-token overlap exists so an idea straddling a chunk boundary -- a sentence that starts at the end of one chunk and finishes at the start of the next -- still appears whole in at least one of the two.

## Step 4 -- Define the metadata every chunk must carry

```text
chunk_id     -- unique per chunk (filename + chunk index)
content      -- the chunk's actual text
filename     -- exact blob path, e.g. "it-wiki/vpn-troubleshooting.html"
source_set   -- "hr-policies" | "it-wiki" | "ops-sops"
position     -- page number (PDFs) or section/heading (wiki pages)
```

Without `filename` and `source_set` on every chunk, a retrieved answer can never be traced back to a real document -- and without that traceability, neither the citation feature nor the evaluation plan two lessons from now has anything to point at.

## Step 5 -- Sketch the pipeline shape end to end

```text
for each folder in [hr-policies/, it-wiki/, ops-sops/]:
    list every blob under that folder prefix
    for each blob:
        download it
        parse it into plain text (format depends on file type)
        split the text into ~500-token chunks, 50-token overlap
        attach filename / source_set / position to every chunk
    write all chunks out, ready for embedding (next build step)
```

## Step 6 -- Walk it past Priya and Omar before building anything

Jordan brings this plan back to Priya and Omar, not just Lena Ortiz: "every document in your folder becomes searchable, as-is, with no manual review on our end -- is that right for how your team actually maintains these folders?" Both confirm it is. That confirmation, plus the written scope decision from Step 2, is what this lesson locks in before a line of ingestion code gets written in the next implementation lesson.

lessons.title: Planning How We'd Actually Know the Answers Are Good
lessons.summary: Before any retrieval or generation code exists, planning how its quality actually gets judged -- a small labeled set of real sample questions per document source, scored on two separate questions: did retrieval find the right chunk, and is the generated answer actually grounded in it.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
A system that answers HR, IT, and Ops questions is worthless if nobody can say with any confidence whether its answers are actually right. This lesson is where Jordan plans how that gets judged -- before the embedding pipeline, the search index, or the GPT-4o prompt exist to be judged. The plan separates two different failure modes that get conflated far too often: retrieval failure (the system searched `wrenfield-knowledge-index` and the right chunk never showed up in the top 5) and generation failure (the right chunk was retrieved, but GPT-4o's answer doesn't actually say what that chunk says). Those are different bugs with different fixes, and testing them together hides which one is actually broken.

The plan itself is a small, labeled evaluation set -- real sample questions pulled from each of the three document sources, each one paired with the document it should be answered from -- scored by hand against both questions above. This lesson states the approach only. No eval set has been built yet, no numbers exist, and nothing here claims the system is already passing anything.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine you've built a robot librarian that's supposed to find the right book on the shelf and then read you the correct answer from it. If the robot gives you a wrong answer, there are two very different reasons that could have happened: maybe it grabbed the wrong book off the shelf entirely, or maybe it grabbed the right book but then told you something that isn't actually written in it. You'd want to know which one happened, because the fix is completely different -- better shelf-organizing versus better reading comprehension.

That's exactly what this lesson plans for Wrenfield's assistant. Before building the actual search-and-answer system, Jordan plans a small test: write down a handful of real questions people would actually ask HR, IT, and Ops, note which real document holds the true answer to each one, and later check both things separately -- did the system pull the right document, and did it then actually say what that document says, instead of making something up. Nothing's been tested yet; this lesson is just deciding how the testing will work.
lessons.explainProfessional:
The plan's central design choice is decomposing evaluation into retrieval quality and generation groundedness as two separate, independently scoreable axes, rather than one end-to-end "was the final answer good" judgment that obscures which stage actually failed. For retrieval, the plan is: for each labeled question, check whether at least one of the top-5 chunks `wrenfield-knowledge-index` returns comes from the document known to contain the real answer. That's a binary, cheap-to-score check per question, and it isolates the embedding/search stage from everything downstream of it.

For generation, the plan asks a narrower, harder question: given the chunks that were actually retrieved, does GPT-4o's answer say only things those chunks support, or does it add claims the retrieved content never made? This is groundedness, not correctness in some absolute sense -- a technically true statement that the retrieved chunks never actually said is still a grounding failure, because it means the model is answering from its own general knowledge or inference rather than from Wrenfield's real documents, which is exactly the failure mode a retrieval-augmented system exists to prevent. The plan calls for building this eval set from real, representative questions sourced from the people who actually field them -- a handful from Priya's HR team, a handful from Omar's IT team, a handful from the Ops team -- each one labeled with the specific document that should answer it, rather than questions Jordan invents in isolation that may not resemble what employees actually ask. Scoring in this first pass is planned as a manual review -- a person reading each retrieved-chunk-and-answer pair and marking it against the two checks above -- with the explicit understanding that this is a starting methodology, not a guarantee that scoring stays manual forever, and with no claim yet about how many questions will be in the set or what any score will come out to. Those are results for a later lesson, once there's an actual pipeline to run the eval set against.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Separate the two things that can go wrong

```text
RETRIEVAL FAILURE
  The right document existed, but wrenfield-knowledge-index's
  top-5 results for this question didn't include a chunk from it.

GENERATION FAILURE
  The right chunk WAS retrieved, but GPT-4o's answer says something
  that chunk doesn't actually support.
```

Testing only the final answer can't tell these apart -- a bad final answer could be either one, or both, and the fix for each is completely different.

## Step 2 -- Plan the labeled question set, sourced from the real teams

```text
For each document source, gather real sample questions from the
people who actually field them:

  hr-policies/   -- sample questions from Priya Desai's HR team
  it-wiki/       -- sample questions from Omar Haddad's IT team
  ops-sops/      -- sample questions from the Ops team

Each question gets labeled with the specific source document that
should answer it -- not just the folder, the exact document.
```

Sourcing questions from the teams themselves, rather than inventing them, matters because the real value of this system depends on handling the questions people actually ask, not a tidy set of textbook examples.

## Step 3 -- Plan the retrieval check

```text
For each labeled question:
  run it through retrieval against wrenfield-knowledge-index (top-k=5)
  check: does at least one of the 5 returned chunks come from the
         labeled correct document?
  record: PASS / FAIL
```

## Step 4 -- Plan the groundedness check

```text
For each labeled question, given the chunks retrieval actually returned:
  generate an answer with GPT-4o
  a reviewer reads the retrieved chunks and the generated answer side
  by side and asks: does every claim in this answer trace back to
  something the retrieved chunks actually say?
  record: GROUNDED / NOT GROUNDED, with a note on what, if anything,
          the answer added that the chunks didn't support
```

## Step 5 -- Plan how this gets reviewed and by whom

The first pass is planned as manual review -- a person reads each pair and scores both checks by hand. That's deliberately the starting point, not a long-term plan to scale to: Jordan notes that once there's a larger question set, a faster scoring approach (sampling, or an LLM-assisted first pass still spot-checked by a person) is worth revisiting, but that's a future decision, not one this lesson makes now.

## Step 6 -- Name what this lesson explicitly does not claim

```text
NOT YET DONE:
  - No eval question set has been written
  - No retrieval or generation code has been run against one
  - No pass rate, score, or number of any kind exists

This lesson plans the method only. Results come once there's an
actual pipeline -- built in later lessons -- to run it against.
```

Jordan brings this plan to Priya and Omar directly, asking each for a first batch of real sample questions once the pipeline exists to test against -- closing the loop between "here's how we'll know it's working" and the people who'll actually be asking it questions.

First-pass scoring is manual. No eval set exists yet and no numbers are claimed -- this is methodology only.

lessons.title: Planning Security, Access, and Deployment
lessons.summary: Planning who inside Wrenfield can query which document sets, how the FastAPI backend actually ships -- Docker, Azure Container Apps, Caleb Shaw's rollout process -- and a standing intention to periodically red-team the system's outputs before and after any change goes live.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Two different kinds of planning happen in this lesson, and Jordan handles them with two different people. With Lena Ortiz, Wrenfield's Security & Compliance Lead, the question is access: now that HR policies, IT wiki pages, and Ops SOPs are all becoming queryable through one assistant, does every one of Wrenfield's roughly 2,200 employees see all three document sets, or should some of them -- Ops SOPs in particular, since they describe internal operational procedures rather than general-audience policy -- be scoped to a narrower audience? With Caleb Shaw, the Platform/DevOps Engineer, the question is deployment: how does the FastAPI backend behind the `/ask` endpoint actually get built, shipped, and updated in Azure Container Apps without Caleb's team babysitting every release by hand.

The lesson closes with one more piece of planning that sits between those two conversations: a standing intention, agreed to but not yet executed, for Lena's team to periodically red-team the system's real outputs and monitor what it actually says to real questions -- not because any specific problem has been found yet, but because a system that answers questions pulled from live, less-curated sources like `it-wiki/` deserves an ongoing check, not just a one-time security sign-off before launch.
lessons.explainSimple:
Picture a company building, with three different filing rooms -- one for HR paperwork, one for IT notes, one for operations procedures. Before giving everyone in the building a master key, somebody sensible asks: should the operations room, specifically, be open to absolutely everyone, or does it make more sense for the people who actually run operations to have the key, and everyone else to ask through them? That's one half of this lesson's planning -- deciding who gets to walk through which door.

The other half is about how a finished product actually gets delivered and updated without someone driving it over by hand every time something changes. Caleb Shaw plans how the system gets packed into a shipping container (literally, in software terms -- a Docker container) that can be dropped into Azure's hosting service and swapped out cleanly for a newer version whenever the team improves something. And on top of both of those plans, the team agrees to a standing habit: periodically sit down and actually test what the assistant says to real, sometimes tricky questions -- not because anything's known to be wrong, but because checking regularly is just good practice for a system this many people will rely on.
lessons.explainProfessional:
The access-scoping conversation with Lena doesn't have one obviously correct answer, and the plan treats it that way rather than defaulting to maximal openness or maximal restriction without reasoning through it. The case for open access across all three document sets is that none of `hr-policies/`, `it-wiki/`, or `ops-sops/` contains anything confidential by Wrenfield's own classification -- these are documents every employee could already request from the owning team today, just inconveniently. The case for scoping `ops-sops/` more narrowly is that operational procedure detail, while not confidential, is also not something a warehouse associate asking an HR question needs surfaced to them by default, and narrower exposure is generally safer exposure. The plan Jordan and Lena land on for V1 is to ship with all three sets visible company-wide -- consistent with the documents' existing, already-open internal availability -- while explicitly flagging access scoping as a decision to revisit as real usage patterns emerge, not a question considered permanently closed.

The deployment plan with Caleb is more mechanical but no less deliberate. The FastAPI application exposing the `/ask` endpoint gets packaged into a Docker image, pushed to a container registry, and deployed to Azure Container Apps -- chosen over a raw VM or an AKS cluster because Container Apps gives Caleb's team managed scaling and revision-based deployments without the operational overhead of running Kubernetes for a single backend service. The rollout plan specifically uses Container Apps' revision model: a new image version ships as a new revision, traffic shifts to it gradually (or all at once for a low-risk change), and the previous revision stays available for an immediate rollback if something's wrong -- rather than a hard cutover with no path back. Layered on top of both plans is Lena's standing commitment to periodic red-teaming and output monitoring -- a recurring practice of actually reading what the system tells real users, checked against expectations, precisely because a system built on indexed content from less-curated sources like a 310-page wiki export is worth watching on an ongoing basis, not just clearing once before launch and assuming it stays correct forever.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Frame the access question honestly, with Lena

```text
ACCESS QUESTION: should all three document sets be visible to every
Wrenfield employee, or should any of them be scoped more narrowly?

FOR open access (all 3 sets, all employees):
  - None of the three folders is classified as confidential today
  - Employees can already request any of these documents from the
    owning team -- this just removes the inconvenience, not a barrier
  - Simpler to build, reason about, and support for V1

FOR scoping ops-sops/ more narrowly:
```

lessons.title: Building the Document Ingestion Pipeline
lessons.summary: Real Python code pulling every file out of the three folders in wrenfield-knowledge-docs, parsing PDFs, HTML wiki exports, and Word SOPs into plain text, chunking each one at roughly 500 tokens with 50-token overlap, and attaching filename/source-set/position metadata to every chunk -- exactly the 'ingest everything in the folder' design from the planning lesson, now actually built.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Planning is done; this lesson is where Jordan actually writes the ingestion pipeline against the real Azure Blob Storage container, `wrenfield-knowledge-docs`. The code walks all three folders -- `hr-policies/`, `it-wiki/`, `ops-sops/` -- downloads every blob it finds under each prefix, parses it into plain text based on its file type (PDF, HTML, or Word), splits that text into roughly 500-token chunks with a 50-token overlap, and attaches the metadata the design lesson specified: `filename`, `source_set`, and a position marker.

This is built exactly as planned: every file under every folder gets pulled in, with no filtering by document status, freshness, or any other property beyond simply belonging to one of the three folders. That's the same reasonable V1 simplification from the design lesson, not a shortcut introduced at build time -- the code below is a straightforward, working implementation of "ingest everything in the folder," ready to hand its output to the embedding step in the next build stage.
lessons.explainSimple:
This is the lesson where the plan from before actually becomes real, running code. Jordan writes a program that connects to Wrenfield's document storage, walks into each of the three folders one at a time, picks up every single file sitting inside, and figures out how to turn it into plain readable text -- PDFs get their text pulled out one way, wiki pages (which are really just web pages) get their text pulled out a different way, and Word documents a third way. Once it has plain text, the program cuts it into chunks of about 500 words with a little overlap between neighbors, and staples a label onto every chunk saying which file it came from and roughly where in that file it sat.

Nothing in this code decides that some files matter more than others, or skips anything -- it just takes everything in each folder, exactly the way the planning lesson said it would, and turns it into labeled, bite-sized pieces ready for the next step.
lessons.explainProfessional:
The implementation follows the design lesson's scope decision literally: enumerate every blob under each of the three folder prefixes, with no status, metadata, or freshness filter applied anywhere in the code. Parsing branches on file extension -- `pdfplumber` extracts text page-by-page from the PDFs in `hr-policies/` and the PDF subset of `ops-sops/` (tracking page number for the position metadata), `BeautifulSoup` strips the Confluence HTML export markup in `it-wiki/` down to its readable text while preserving the page's heading as a section marker, and `python-docx` pulls paragraph text from the Word-format SOPs in `ops-sops/`. Chunking uses `tiktoken`'s `cl100k_base` encoding to operate on actual token counts rather than a word or character proxy, sliding a 500-token window across each document's token stream with a 50-token step-back between windows to produce the overlap.

Every resulting chunk is written out as a flat record -- `chunk_id`, `content`, `filename`, `source_set`, `position` -- staged to a local JSONL file in this lesson, ready for the embedding step (Azure OpenAI `text-embedding-3-small`) that a later build lesson will run against this exact output. The code intentionally contains no logic that inspects a document's title, header, status, or any other in-document signal to decide whether it should be treated differently from the rest of its folder -- every file found under a given prefix is ingested the same way, because nothing in this project has yet identified a reason to do otherwise, and building that kind of filtering speculatively, before any real need for it has surfaced, isn't where V1's effort is best spent.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Connect to the container and enumerate the three folders

```python
from azure.storage.blob import ContainerClient

CONNECTION_STRING = "<wrenfield storage account connection string>"
CONTAINER_NAME = "wrenfield-knowledge-docs"
FOLDERS = {
    "hr-policies/": "hr-policies",
    "it-wiki/": "it-wiki",
    "ops-sops/": "ops-sops",
}

container_client = ContainerClient.from_connection_string(
    CONNECTION_STRING, container_name=CONTAINER_NAME
)

def list_folder_blobs(prefix):
    return list(container_client.list_blobs(name_starts_with=prefix))
```

Every blob under every one of the three prefixes gets listed -- there's no check against a status field, a last-modified cutoff, or anything else beyond folder membership.

## Step 2 -- Parse each file type into plain text

```python
import pdfplumber, docx, io
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup

def extract_pdf(blob_bytes):
    pages = []
    with pdfplumber.open(io.BytesIO(blob_bytes)) as pdf:
        for i, page in enumerate(pdf.pages):
            pages.append((i + 1, page.extract_text() or ""))
    return pages  # [(page_number, text), ...]

def extract_html(blob_bytes):
    soup = BeautifulSoup(blob_bytes, "html.parser")
    heading = soup.find(["h1", "h2"])
    section = heading.get_text(strip=True) if heading else "untitled"
    text = soup.get_text(separator="\n", strip=True)
    return [(section, text)]

def extract_docx(blob_bytes):
    doc = docx.Document(io.BytesIO(blob_bytes))
    text = "\n".join(p.text for p in doc.paragraphs)
    return [("document", text)]

def extract_text(filename, blob_bytes):
    ext = filename.lower().rsplit(".", 1)[-1]
    if ext == "pdf":
        return extract_pdf(blob_bytes)
    if ext in ("html", "htm"):
        return extract_html(blob_bytes)
    if ext == "docx":
        return extract_docx(blob_bytes)
    return [("document", blob_bytes.decode("utf-8", errors="ignore"))]
```

## Step 3 -- Chunk by real token count, with overlap

```python
import tiktoken

encoding = tiktoken.get_encoding("cl100k_base")
CHUNK_SIZE = 500
CHUNK_OVERLAP = 50

def chunk_text(text):
    tokens = encoding.encode(text)
    chunks, start = [], 0
    while start < len(tokens):
        end = start + CHUNK_SIZE
        chunks.append(encoding.decode(tokens[start:end]))
        start += CHUNK_SIZE - CHUNK_OVERLAP
    return chunks
```

## Step 4 -- Assemble every chunk with its metadata

```python
import json

def ingest_folder(prefix, source_set):
    records = []
    for blob in list_folder_blobs(prefix):
        blob_bytes = container_client.get_blob_client(blob.name).download_blob().readall()
        for position, text in extract_text(blob.name, blob_bytes):
            for i, chunk in enumerate(chunk_text(text)):
                records.append({
                    "chunk_id": f"{blob.name}::{position}::{i}",
                    "content": chunk,
                    "filename": blob.name,
                    "source_set": source_set,
                    "position": position,
                })
    return records

all_chunks = []
for prefix, source_set in FOLDERS.items():
    all_chunks.extend(ingest_folder(prefix, source_set))

with open("wrenfield_chunks.jsonl", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    for record in all_chunks:
        f.write(json.dumps(record) + "\n")

print(f"Ingested {len(all_chunks)} chunks from {len(FOLDERS)} folders.")
```

## Step 5 -- Spot-check the output before handing it to embedding

Jordan runs the pipeline once against the real container and reads a handful of chunks from each source set by hand: a few from `hr-policies/` to confirm PDF text extraction didn't mangle any policy wording, a few from `it-wiki/` to confirm the HTML stripping left readable sentences rather than leftover markup, and a few from `ops-sops/` to confirm both the PDF and Word SOPs came through cleanly. The chunk count -- several thousand chunks across all three folders -- and a quick scan of `source_set` value counts confirm all three folders actually got walked, not just one:

```python
import collections

counts = collections.Counter(r["source_set"] for r in all_chunks)
print(counts)
# Counter({'it-wiki': 2114, 'hr-policies': 1189, 'ops-sops': 702})
```

Those three counts roughly track the folder's file counts scaled up by average document length, which is the quick gut-check Jordan uses to confirm nothing silently failed partway through a folder -- a zero or a suspiciously tiny count for any one of the three would mean that folder's listing or parsing broke somewhere upstream.

## Step 6 -- Hand the output forward

`wrenfield_chunks.jsonl` is this lesson's deliverable -- every file in all three folders, parsed, chunked, and labeled, exactly as the design lesson scoped it. The next build step takes this file and runs each chunk's content through Azure OpenAI's `text-embedding-3-small` model, then loads the result into `wrenfield-knowledge-index`.

No filtering beyond folder membership, exactly as scoped. Output staged to wrenfield_chunks.jsonl for the embedding step.

lessons.title: Generating Embeddings and Building the Vector Index
lessons.summary: Every chunk ingestion produced gets embedded with Azure OpenAI text-embedding-3-small and pushed into a hybrid vector+keyword Azure AI Search index -- no filtering, no exceptions, so the index faithfully mirrors everything lesson 8 pulled out of Blob Storage.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding: Lesson 8 built the ingestion pipeline that reads every file out of the three `wrenfield-knowledge-docs` folders (`hr-policies/`, `it-wiki/`, `ops-sops/`) in Azure Blob Storage and splits it into roughly 500-token chunks with a 50-token overlap, writing the result out as one row per chunk with its source path and chunk id attached. This lesson is where those chunks actually become searchable: Jordan Vance calls Azure OpenAI's `text-embedding-3-small` model on every single chunk ingestion produced, then pushes the resulting 1536-dimension vectors, together with the chunk text and its metadata, into a brand-new Azure AI Search index named `wrenfield-knowledge-index`, configured for hybrid search -- vector similarity and traditional keyword search running side by side on the same index. The rule for this lesson is simple and non-negotiable: every chunk that came out of lesson 8's ingestion gets embedded and indexed. Nothing gets excluded, screened, or deduplicated based on where it came from or what folder it sat in -- the index is meant to be a faithful, complete mirror of what ingestion produced, not a curated subset of it.
lessons.explainSimple: Imagine a library where every book just got printed, but none of them are catalogued yet -- you have a huge pile of pages with no way to search any of it. This lesson is the librarian's job: turning every single page that came out of all those HR, IT, and operations documents into a tiny searchable "fingerprint" -- a long list of numbers that captures roughly what that page is about -- and filing it into a card catalog anyone can search by typing a plain-English question. Every chunk ingestion produced gets a fingerprint and gets filed. The job right now is to catalog everything completely and accurately, not to decide which pages matter most -- that judgment call, if it's ever needed, belongs to a later step.
lessons.explainProfessional:
A text embedding is a fixed-length vector -- 1536 floats for `text-embedding-3-small` -- positioned in a high-dimensional space such that semantically similar text lands near other semantically similar text, regardless of exact wording. That's what lets Azure AI Search answer a question phrased one way against a document chunk phrased a completely different way, which a pure keyword index can't do. Hybrid search keeps both: a vector similarity component for paraphrase-tolerant semantic matching, and a traditional keyword component that still catches exact terms -- acronyms, policy codes, extension numbers -- that an embedding alone can blur together. Wrenfield's index runs both simultaneously and merges the ranked results, which is why it's configured as hybrid rather than vector-only from the start.

The scope decision for this lesson is deliberately simple: every chunk lesson 8's ingestion produced across `hr-policies/`, `it-wiki/`, and `ops-sops/` gets embedded and written to the index, full stop. No per-document review, no content classification, no staleness check on modification dates, no folder-based inclusion rules. That's a reasonable v1 decision -- Wrenfield doesn't have a document-governance process yet, and building one is a separate, larger project than standing up search itself.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Load lesson 8's chunk output

```python
import json

CHUNKS_PATH = "ingested/wrenfield_chunks.jsonl"

chunks = []
with open(CHUNKS_PATH, "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    for line in f:
        chunks.append(json.loads(line))

print(f"Loaded {len(chunks):,} chunks from ingestion")
# Loaded 14,382 chunks from ingestion
```

Each row from lesson 8 already carries `chunk_id`, `source_path` (for example `it-wiki/VPN-Password-Reset-Steps.docx`), `folder`, `text`, and `token_count` -- this lesson embeds and indexes every one of them, exactly as they are.

## Step 2 -- Create the Azure AI Search index schema

```python
from azure.search.documents.indexes import SearchIndexClient
from azure.search.documents.indexes.models import (
    SearchIndex, SimpleField, SearchableField, SearchField,
    SearchFieldDataType, VectorSearch, HnswAlgorithmConfiguration,
    VectorSearchProfile,
)
from azure.core.credentials import AzureKeyCredential

index_client = SearchIndexClient(
    endpoint="https://wrenfield-search.search.windows.net",
    credential=AzureKeyCredential(SEARCH_API_KEY),
)

fields = [
    SimpleField(name="chunk_id", type=SearchFieldDataType.String, key=True),
    SimpleField(name="source_path", type=SearchFieldDataType.String, filterable=True),
    SimpleField(name="folder", type=SearchFieldDataType.String, filterable=True),
    SearchableField(name="text", type=SearchFieldDataType.String),
    SearchField(
        name="content_vector",
        type=SearchFieldDataType.Collection(SearchFieldDataType.Single),
        searchable=True, vector_search_dimensions=1536,
        vector_search_profile_name="wrenfield-hnsw-profile",
    ),
]

vector_search = VectorSearch(
    algorithms=[HnswAlgorithmConfiguration(name="wrenfield-hnsw")],
    profiles=[VectorSearchProfile(name="wrenfield-hnsw-profile", algorithm_configuration_name="wrenfield-hnsw")],
)

index_client.create_or_update_index(
    SearchIndex(name="wrenfield-knowledge-index", fields=fields, vector_search=vector_search)
)
```

`text` stays a plain searchable string field -- that's the keyword half of hybrid search. `content_vector` is where the embedding lands -- that's the vector half. Both exist on the same document, which is what makes a single query able to search both at once.

## Step 3 -- Embed every chunk with text-embedding-3-small

```python
from openai import AzureOpenAI
import time

aoai = AzureOpenAI(
    azure_endpoint="https://wrenfield-openai.openai.azure.com",
    api_key=AOAI_API_KEY, api_version="2024-06-01",
)

def embed_batch(texts, retries=3):
    for attempt in range(retries):
        try:
            resp = aoai.embeddings.create(model="text-embedding-3-small", input=texts)
            return [item.embedding for item in resp.data]
        except Exception as e:
            print(f"Embedding batch failed (attempt {attempt+1}): {e}")
            time.sleep(2 ** attempt)
    raise RuntimeError("Embedding batch failed after retries")

BATCH_SIZE = 100
for i in range(0, len(chunks), BATCH_SIZE):
    batch = chunks[i:i + BATCH_SIZE]
    vectors = embed_batch([c["text"] for c in batch])
    for chunk, vector in zip(batch, vectors):
        chunk["content_vector"] = vector
```

Every chunk gets embedded here, regardless of which folder it came from or what it says -- `hr-policies/`, `it-wiki/`, and `ops-sops/` chunks all go through the exact same loop.

## Step 4 -- Upload to the index in batches

```python
from azure.search.documents import SearchClient

search_client = SearchClient(
    endpoint="https://wrenfield-search.search.windows.net",
    index_name="wrenfield-knowledge-index",
    credential=AzureKeyCredential(SEARCH_API_KEY),
)

for i in range(0, len(chunks), BATCH_SIZE):
    batch = chunks[i:i + BATCH_SIZE]
    docs = [
        {"chunk_id": c["chunk_id"], "source_path": c["source_path"],
         "folder": c["folder"], "text": c["text"], "content_vector": c["content_vector"]}
        for c in batch
    ]
    result = search_client.upload_documents(documents=docs)
    failed = [r for r in result if not r.succeeded]
    if failed:
        print(f"{len(failed)} documents failed to index in this batch")
```

## Step 5 -- Confirm the index matches ingestion exactly

```python
doc_count = search_client.get_document_count()
print(f"Indexed documents: {doc_count:,} | Chunks from ingestion: {len(chunks):,}")
# Indexed documents: 14,382 | Chunks from ingestion: 14,382
```

The two numbers matching is the whole point of this lesson: `wrenfield-knowledge-index` now holds a complete, embedded, hybrid-searchable copy of every chunk lesson 8's ingestion pipeline produced across all three Blob Storage folders -- nothing held back, nothing pre-screened.

## Step 6 -- Hand off the running cost and the refresh cadence to Caleb Shaw

Embedding roughly 14,400 chunks is a real, metered cost -- `text-embedding-3-small` is priced per token, and at an average of around 420 tokens per chunk this first full run works out to a modest but non-trivial one-time bill, plus whatever runs again every time ingestion picks up new or changed documents. Caleb Shaw, who owns the Container Apps environment this whole pipeline eventually deploys into, schedules the embed-and-index job in this lesson to re-run nightly as new or edited files land in `wrenfield-knowledge-docs`, rather than re-embedding all 14,400 chunks from scratch every time -- the nightly job diffs against `chunk_id`s already present in the index and only embeds what's new. Jordan and Caleb also settle on `wrenfield-hnsw` (approximate nearest-neighbor search) over an exhaustive k-nearest-neighbor configuration for the vector field: HNSW trades a small amount of recall for a large reduction in query latency, which matters once real employees are waiting on an answer rather than a batch job running overnight. Both decisions get written into the same short runbook Caleb already keeps for the ingestion job, so the whole pipeline -- ingest, embed, index -- is documented as one continuous process rather than three separate ones.

No filtering applied anywhere in this step -- every chunk from hr-policies/, it-wiki/, and ops-sops/ went through the same embed-and-upload loop, and the indexed document count matches the ingested chunk count exactly. Caleb's scheduling this to re-run nightly.

lessons.title: Building Retrieval and Prompt Assembly
lessons.summary: Given a user's question, embed it the same way, query wrenfield-knowledge-index for the top-5 hybrid-matched chunks, and assemble them into one context block ready to hand to a prompt -- the retrieval mechanics this whole assistant depends on, not yet the system prompt itself.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding: Lesson 9 made every chunk in `wrenfield-knowledge-index` searchable. This lesson builds the other half of retrieval: given a real question typed by a Wrenfield employee, turn that question into the same kind of embedding lesson 9 built for every chunk, send it to Azure AI Search as a hybrid query against `wrenfield-knowledge-index`, pull back the top-5 (`top-k=5`) best-matching chunks by combined vector and keyword relevance, and assemble those five chunks into one clean context block -- source labels and all -- ready to be handed to a prompt. This lesson stops exactly there: the context block gets built and printed, but nothing yet calls GPT-4o or decides how the model should use it. That's lesson 11's job.
lessons.explainSimple: Lesson 9 built the card catalog; this lesson is what happens the moment someone walks up and asks the librarian a real question. First the question itself gets turned into the same kind of fingerprint every page got. Then the librarian compares that fingerprint against the whole catalog and pulls the five cards that match best -- not just the one best match, five, so there's a decent spread of material to work with. Then those five cards get stacked together into one neat packet, each one labeled with which document it came from, ready to hand to whoever answers the question next.
lessons.explainProfessional: Azure AI Search's hybrid query runs the vector similarity search and the keyword search against the same index in one call, then merges the two ranked lists into one final ordering -- which is why the retrieval code only needs to issue a single `search_client.search()` call with both a `vector_queries` argument and a plain `search_text` argument, rather than running two separate queries and merging them by hand. `top=5` is a deliberate choice, not a default: five chunks gives the generation step in lesson 11 enough surrounding context to answer most real questions fully, without ballooning the prompt size or burying the one genuinely relevant chunk among a dozen marginal ones. The embedding model used to embed the incoming question has to be the exact same model used to embed every chunk in lesson 9 -- `text-embedding-3-small` -- because the two sets of vectors only mean anything measured against each other if they were produced by the same model.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Embed the incoming question

```python
def embed_query(question: str) -> list[float]:
    resp = aoai.embeddings.create(model="text-embedding-3-small", input=[question])
    return resp.data[0].embedding
```

Same client, same model as lesson 9 -- a query vector only means something measured against chunk vectors built by the identical model.

## Step 2 -- Run the hybrid search against wrenfield-knowledge-index

```python
from azure.search.documents.models import VectorizedQuery

def retrieve(question: str, k: int = 5):
    query_vector = embed_query(question)
    vector_query = VectorizedQuery(
        vector=query_vector, k_nearest_neighbors=k, fields="content_vector",
    )
    results = search_client.search(
        search_text=question,          # keyword half of hybrid search
        vector_queries=[vector_query], # vector half of hybrid search
        select=["chunk_id", "source_path", "folder", "text"],
        top=k,
    )
    return list(results)
```

Passing both `search_text` and `vector_queries` in the same call is what makes this hybrid rather than vector-only or keyword-only -- Azure AI Search runs both and returns one merged, ranked list of `k` results.

## Step 3 -- Assemble the retrieved chunks into a context block

```python
def assemble_context(results) -> str:
    blocks = []
    for r in results:
        label = f"[{r['source_path']}]"
        blocks.append(f"{label}\n{r['text']}")
    return "\n\n---\n\n".join(blocks)
```

Each chunk keeps its own source label attached, separated by a clear divider -- this is the exact text block lesson 11's prompt wraps around.

## Step 4 -- Try it against real Wrenfield questions

```python
for question in [
    "How do I request access to the VPN?",
    "How many days of PTO carry over at year end?",
    "What's the SOP for a damaged inbound pallet at the dock?",
]:
    results = retrieve(question, k=5)
    print(question)
    for r in results:
        print(f"  matched: {r['source_path']}  (chunk {r['chunk_id']})")
    print()
```

Running this against the live index returns five chunks per question, pulled from across `it-wiki/`, `hr-policies/`, and `ops-sops/` depending on which folder actually holds the relevant material -- the VPN question pulls primarily from `it-wiki/` pages, the PTO question from `hr-policies/` PDFs, and the damaged-pallet question from `ops-sops/` documents. Jordan Vance checks a handful of these by hand against the real source documents in Blob Storage to confirm the right material is actually coming back before moving on.

## Step 5 -- Package retrieval as one callable function

```python
def get_context_for_question(question: str, k: int = 5) -> tuple[str, list[dict]]:
    results = retrieve(question, k=k)
    context = assemble_context(results)
    return context, results
```

Returning both the assembled context string and the raw result list matters -- lesson 11 needs the context string for the prompt, and lesson 12 needs the raw results (their scores and `source_path` metadata) for citations and the confidence check.

## Step 6 -- Why five, and why this is still just mechanics

`top-k=5` isn't an arbitrary number -- it's the same figure fixed back when Jordan scoped the architecture, chosen as a balance point: fewer than five risks missing the one chunk that actually answers a multi-part question (a VPN question that depends on both an eligibility rule in one wiki page and a setup procedure in another, for instance), while meaningfully more than five starts diluting the context block with marginal matches and pushing up both token cost and GPT-4o's response latency on every single question. Jordan deliberately stops this lesson at the context block itself -- no system prompt, no model call, no decision yet about how an AI consuming this context should treat it. That's a clean handoff: lesson 10 guarantees the five best-matching chunks for any question, correctly labeled by source, and lesson 11 picks up from exactly that point to decide what to do with them.

lessons.explainProfessional: A system prompt for a retrieval-augmented assistant has one central job: tell the model what it's for, what material it's allowed to draw on, and roughly how to phrase the answer.
